Croxton
KROKS-tun
n. (the Leicestershire Premonstratensian abbey of 1160, where King John's body was embalmed)
Old English Croc, a personal name, and tun, an enclosure; Croc's farmstead.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Croxton Kerrial in Leicestershire was founded about 1160 and became one of the wealthier Premonstratensian houses in England. Its abbot was physician to King John, and when the king died at Newark in October 1216 the abbot embalmed the body; John's bowels were buried at Croxton and the rest of him carried to Worcester. The abbey was dissolved in 1538 and almost nothing remains above ground. This dictionary records Croxton for that grim errand, because the embalming of a king is a blunt reminder of what Scripture says happens to every body including the powerful. The sentence is passed in Eden and is universal, “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19). The Preacher states it as a separation, “Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecc 12:7). Man's days are compared to grass, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15), and against all of it Job expects to stand up again in a body, “I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth” (Job 19:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to embalm as to fill a dead body with spices to preserve it; a corpse as the dead body of a human being; dust as fine dry particles of earth; mortality as subjection to death; and the grave as the place of the dead.

expand to see more

EMBALM, v.t. To open a dead body, take out the intestines, and fill their place with odoriferous and desiccative spices and drugs, to prevent its putrefaction.

CORPSE, n. The dead body of a human being.

DUST, n. Fine dry particles of earth or other matter, so attenuated that it may be raised and wafted by the wind; earth; the grave.

MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death or the necessity of dying; death; also, frequency of death.

GRAVE, n. A pit or deep place in the earth; the place or receptacle of the dead; the sepulchre.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:19 — "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

Ecc 12:7 — "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it."

Psa 103:15 — "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth."

Job 19:25 — "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:"

Modern Corruption

Leicestershire Premonstratensian abbey of 1160: its abbot was King John's physician and embalmed him at Newark in 1216.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the levelling plainness of the sentence. Embalming is an attempt to delay what Scripture states without exception, and the words are addressed to the first man rather than to a criminal, “for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19). The Preacher separates the two halves of a man and sends each where it came from, “and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecc 12:7).

The second thing is the hope that is not a denial. The psalm's comparison is not meant as consolation, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15), and Scripture never softens it. What it adds instead is a person and a day, in words Job spoke without any of the apparatus of later theology, “I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25). An abbey keeping a king's entrails under its floor and a parish reciting Job both had the matter about right.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'aphar (H6083), dust; Hebrew ruach (H7307), spirit; Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass; Hebrew go'el (H1350), a redeemer; Hebrew shub (H7725), to return.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'aphar (H6083) — dust, both origin and end; “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return”, Genesis 3:19.

Hebrew shub (H7725) — to return to where one came from; “Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was”, Ecclesiastes 12:7.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, returning to the giver; “and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it”, Ecclesiastes 12:7.

Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, the measure of a life; “As for man, his days are as grass”, Psalm 103:15.

Hebrew go'el (H1350) — a redeemer, who lives; “I know that my redeemer liveth”, Job 19:25.

Usage

"“dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19) — said to the first man, not to a criminal."

"“and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecc 12:7) — the two halves, each sent home."

"“I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25) — hope that does not deny the dust."
